newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Malan case judge calls key state witness liar.
newsitem.headline: Malan case judge calls key state witness liar.

text.p: A South African judge trying apartheid-era defence minister Magnus Malan for murder branded one crucial prosecution witness a liar and two others unreliable as he began to pass judgment on Thursday.

Malan, the most senior figure from the old white regime to be charged with atrocities against political opponents, sat in court in Durban with 15 others, including army generals, accused with him of ordering or carrying out the 1987 massacre of 13 blacks.

Judge Jan Hugo said some evidence supported the defence view that Malan and apartheid's generals had no links with the attack they called a "frolic" that was run solely by Johan Opperman. Opperman and two other military officers testified in the hope of avoiding prosecution.
The judge said Opperman's contradictory claims in court went "some way towards the view that the military neither planned nor approved the attack".

The judge attacked the prosecution case, saying some evidence was misleading -- "probably deliberately" -- and that surprisingly few witnesses had been called who might have been able to back up claims by Opperman and the other two key witnesses.
The court had to be aware that the three were "self- confessed criminals who are trying to get some benefits by testifying... red lights must necessarily start flashing", Hugo said.
"We would have greatly doubted their veracity, even if they were not accomplices," he added.
The defendants joked and looked relaxed and supporters said they were confident that Hugo's remarks were building up to acquittal by Friday at the latest.
Malan sat in a blue suit alongside the grey-haired generals he is accused with, taking notes and retaining his well-known stern expression.
Hugo said the landmark trial would regrettably leave unanswered many of the questions it raised.

The judge said Opperman, probably the most important witness in the case against Malan and the others, had made out he was a slick military operator when in reality he was an administrator who the army was unlikely to have left in charge.

Opperman claimed he was in charge of the attack on the home of black activist Victor Ntuli near the Indian Ocean port of Durban. Ntuli was not at home during the attack but 13 family and friends, six of them children, were killed.

Malan, head of the armed forces before he entered the cabinet, admits he helped set up a para-military force for the Zulu-based Inkatha party, the main black rival of Nelson Mandela's African National Congress.
But he says the force was legitimate and that if it had any hand in the massacre, he knew nothing about it.
Acquittal would be welcomed by supporters of the old government, who have called the trial a witch hunt.

Those who suffered under apartheid say a not-guilty verdict for Malan, who led the white government's war against black opponents, would deal a heavy setback to South Africa's efforts to punish the crimes of the past.
Four of the original 20 accused were acquitted earlier because of lack of evidence against them.
